title: Your Ads Are About to Send Customers Somewhere New First. Here's What to Check Before October 28.
body: Last updated October 22, 2026. We'll update this if Meta publishes an official page on the change. Right now, when someone taps your Facebook or Instagram ad, they land on your website. Starting October 28, Meta Product Browsing changes that by default for a lot of advertisers already running ads. What happened Meta's notice to advertisers says it plainly: "Starting October 28, 2026, we'll add product browsing to your existing ads." Instead of going straight from an ad tap to your website, shoppers may first see an in-app page on Facebook or Instagram built from your product catalog, pricing, and images, plus personalized suggestions based on their own shopping behavior. They can still click through to your site from there, but the direct path is gone unless you opt out first. The notice reportedly started circulating with advertisers around October 14, giving about two weeks before the default flips on October 28, which lands almost exactly 30 days before Black Friday. What Meta says it does Meta says its own 16-day experiment August 6 to 21, 2026 across roughly 117,700 advertisers in e-commerce, CPG, and retail, showed 3% more conversions on average with Product Browsing turned on, at better than 99% statistical confidence. That's Meta's own reported claim, not an independently verified result; Meta hasn't published its methodology, so it's not clear how conversions were defined, how comparison groups were built, or what happened to cost per result or revenue, not just conversion count. A 3% average across tens of thousands of accounts also doesn't guarantee anything about your specific account, your catalog, or your audience. A note on where this information is coming from The primary source here is Meta's own notice to advertisers, quoted above. As of this writing, Meta hasn't published that notice as a public Help Center article, blog post, or newsroom announcement, so what's available is the notice itself, as reported by PPC Land https://ppc.land/meta-will-turn-on-product-browsing-in-existing-ads-on-october-28/ and corroborated independently by other ad-industry outlets. Worth checking Meta's own Ads Manager and Help Center directly for your account before October 28, in case anything has been clarified or changed since this was written. We'll update this article if Meta publishes an official public page. Why it matters, especially right now Adding a step between the ad tap and your website changes your funnel, even if the end result is a sale. You lose a direct, trackable site visit in exchange for an in-app experience you don't fully control, including personalized product suggestions that advertisers have flagged as a risk if your own catalog is incomplete or your margins depend on exactly what a shopper sees first. And the timing is the part worth sitting with: this turns on 30 days before Black Friday, right as most small businesses are finalizing the exact campaigns this would apply to. If your ads already point to a strong, fast, well-merchandised product catalog, this might genuinely help. If you're running lifestyle or brand-awareness ads without a catalog behind them, or your site experience is a meaningful part of why people buy from you, this is worth testing before you assume it's neutral or good. How to opt out of Meta product browsing 1. Use the "Opt out" button in Meta's notice to your account advertisers describe receiving this by email , before October 28, 2026. 2. Or turn it off per ad , anytime, in that ad's Advantage+ Creative and Destination settings. You can change this setting at any time, before or after October 28, it isn't a one-time, irreversible choice. No bulk, account-wide opt-out has been confirmed publicly as of this writing, so if you manage several ad accounts or a lot of active ads, budget time to check more than one. What to actually do before October 28 Audit your product catalog in Commerce Manager now: pricing, images, and descriptions all feed directly into what shoppers see in this experience. If you want real data instead of guessing, run a short side-by-side test first, Product Browsing on for part of your budget, off for the rest, using your own conversion and revenue numbers rather than Meta's reported average. And set a baseline now for how much traffic actually reaches your website from ads, so you can tell later whether this changed it. What not to overreact to This isn't Meta hiding a price increase or quietly taking money from you. It's a UX change to the click path, it's reversible per ad at any time, and if your catalog and offer are strong, the in-app experience might convert just as well or better. The 3% figure is also an average, not a guarantee, so the right response is to test it against your own numbers, not to assume it will help or hurt before you've checked. What to watch next Two things nobody can answer yet, including us: whether new ads created after October 28 also default to Product Browsing being on is unknown , since Meta's notice doesn't say either way, and whether Meta ever publishes an official page on this the way it usually does for changes this size. Until then, the in-app notice and your own test results are the most reliable things to go on. The bigger lesson here This is the same pattern as a platform changing what counts as a billable lead or auto-upgrading your campaign settings: something about how your ads work changes by default, and you only notice if you were paying attention that week. The habit worth building isn't checking every platform every day. It's knowing where each platform tends to post these changes, and setting a reminder to check before a date like this one. Sources & Further Reading - Meta's notice to advertisers quoted above , as reported by PPC Land https://ppc.land/meta-will-turn-on-product-browsing-in-existing-ads-on-october-28/ , the primary evidence for this article - Meta will turn on product browsing in existing ads on 28 October 2026 https://www.relevantaudience.com/meta/meta-product-browsing-existing-ads-october-28/ , Relevant Audience independent corroboration - Meta Is Auto-Enabling Product Browsing in Your Existing Ads on October 28 https://commonthreadco.com/blogs/coachs-corner/meta-is-auto-enabling-product-browsing-in-your-existing-ads-on-october-28-what-ecommerce-brands-must-do-before-black-friday , Common Thread Co independent corroboration How Lonko looks at this Meta changed what happens after someone clicks your ad without asking first, and that's exactly the kind of change we want Lonko to help businesses catch. Lonko is in development today, with a private reference version running on Google Ads; LinkedIn Ads is next, and every action still requires human approval before it touches your account. More on what we're building /about/ , plus related coverage on Insights /insights/ and our take on Google's Local Services Ads billing change /chronicles/local-services-ads-new-billing-rules-what-changed/ . title: OpenAI Opened ChatGPT Ads to Every Business. Here's What's Real and What's Still Unproven.
body: A year ago, running ads inside ChatGPT wasn't something most small businesses could even ask about. The pilot program was invite-only, and the minimum spend to get in the door was $50,000. That's no longer true. Over the past several months, OpenAI has quietly opened advertising on ChatGPT to any business willing to sign up, dropped the budget floor that kept smaller advertisers out, and built the pieces reporting partners, a Shopify app, a creative toolkit that make it look less like an experiment and more like a real channel. If you're wondering whether this is something your business should actually test, or just another AI headline to skim past, here's what's confirmed, what's still early, and what's worth watching before you spend a dollar on it. What happened OpenAI rolled this out in stages across 2026, not all at once, which is part of why it's easy to have missed. In January, OpenAI confirmed ads were coming to ChatGPT for adult users in the US, kept clearly labeled and separate from the chatbot's answers. By May, it opened a public beta of its Ads Manager and dropped the $50,000 minimum spend that had limited the earlier pilot to large advertisers working directly with OpenAI's sales team, a change OpenAI's own monetization lead framed as opening the platform to businesses without big budgets or an agency behind them. In September, OpenAI added two features aimed specifically at smaller, less technical advertisers: a ChatGPT Ads for Shopify app that connects directly to a merchant's existing product catalog US merchants first, expanding to other markets later that month , and a HubSpot integration for businesses that manage customers there already. It also introduced Sponsored Agents, still in testing with a small group of US advertisers, where clicking an ad can open a separate, clearly labeled conversation with a business-run AI agent. Most recently, on October 5, OpenAI announced a new visual ad format that appears during image generation in ChatGPT, rolling out this month to Free and Go-plan users, along with a broader measurement push: integrations with attribution platforms like AppsFlyer, Triple Whale, and Northbeam, early incrementality-testing partners, and brand-safety evaluation pilots with DoubleVerify and Integral Ad Science. Put together, this went from a closed, enterprise-only pilot to something close to a self-serve ad platform, with the connective tissue ecommerce integration, measurement, creative tools a real small business would actually need to run it. Why it matters ChatGPT reaches about 1.2 billion people every week, by OpenAI's own figure. Even a sliver of that is a real audience, and arguably one with more purchase intent than a casual social scroll: someone asking ChatGPT to compare running shoes or plan a trip is closer to a buying decision than someone mid-scroll between videos. OpenAI has reportedly set internal targets around $2.5 billion in ad revenue this year and $100 billion by 2030, which signals this isn't a side experiment for them. More practically: every new ad channel goes through a window where early advertisers get cheaper attention than the channel will ever offer again, before competition and ad prices catch up. That's not guaranteed to repeat here, but it's happened with every major platform that opened self-serve advertising, from early Facebook Ads to early TikTok Ads. Whether it's worth jumping on depends on what's actually proven so far, not on how new or interesting it sounds. What's actually proven so far The honest answer: not much yet, and OpenAI's own language reflects that. The strongest results circulating come from OpenAI's measurement partners, reporting on a small number of named brands. WeightWatchers' cost per acquisition on ChatGPT Ads came in 15.3% lower than its blended paid-search benchmark, according to DV Rockerbox. WorkMagic reported that 67% of wellness brand Dose's incremental purchases came from genuinely new customers. Triple Whale found that 93% of visitors Portland Leather got from ChatGPT Ads were new to the brand. Those are promising, but they're a handful of case studies supplied through OpenAI's own measurement-partner program, not independent, broad-based results, and OpenAI's own materials describe its incrementality testing as still in its early stages. Treat these as early signal, not proof this will work for your business or category. What's still unverified or worth watching A few things are worth knowing before treating this as a settled channel. There's no confirmed minimum spend right now, but the platform is still a US-only beta, which limits it if your customers are elsewhere. OpenAI says advertising doesn't influence ChatGPT's own answers, but reporting on the May beta launch has pointed out that OpenAI hasn't published evidence for that claim, and that the platform's billing is moving toward click-based pricing, which would give OpenAI a financial incentive to show ads exactly where someone's making a purchase decision. There's also real outside scrutiny. In January 2026, Senator Edward Markey sent OpenAI and several other AI companies a formal letter raising concerns about ads in chatbots: whether they could be mistaken for the chatbot's own neutral advice, whether sensitive conversations about health or family matters could ever be used for targeting, and whether paid placement could quietly shape what a chatbot recommends. OpenAI has pointed to its stated safeguards labeled ads, no targeting from sensitive conversations, no ads for minors in response, but the specific questions the letter raised haven't been independently verified one way or the other. What to actually do If you're curious, the cost of finding out is low. Sign-up is at ads.openai.com, no large budget is required to get in the door anymore, and if you already sell through Shopify or manage customers in HubSpot, most of the integration work is close to done for you. Treat it like a genuine test, not a channel switch. Run it alongside whatever's already working, with a budget small enough that a disappointing result doesn't actually hurt you, and don't move budget away from a channel you already trust until you have your own data, not someone else's case study, saying it's worth it. What not to overreact to You're not behind. This is weeks old as a self-serve platform, limited to the US, and still missing pieces independent measurement, a track record beyond a handful of showcased brands, clarity on the outstanding privacy questions that take time to resolve. Nothing here means your existing channels stopped working, and nothing here means you need an "AI advertising strategy" by next quarter. It means there's a new option worth a small, low-risk look, not an emergency. What to watch next The real tests ahead: independent data instead of partner-supplied case studies, whether a minimum spend quietly reappears as the platform matures, how OpenAI responds to the specific questions in Senator Markey's letter, and whether the platform expands past the US. If you do test it, measure your own numbers against your other channels, not against OpenAI's own highlighted results. The bigger lesson here Every new advertising channel asks you to decide with incomplete information. Jump in too early and the proof doesn't exist yet. Wait too long and the cheap attention is gone. The honest move isn't picking a side before you have your own data. It's treating the first few months of any new channel as a small, deliberately low-stakes experiment, with a budget you can afford to lose and a clear question you're actually trying to answer, rather than jumping in because it's new or dismissing it because it's unproven. title: Google Changed How Local Services Ads Bills You for Calls. Here's What Actually Shifted.
body: Every advertising platform you use has a quiet rulebook for what you're actually paying for. A "click." A "lead." A "conversion." Most days that rulebook sits in the background and you never think about it. Then the platform rewrites a line in it, and your bill changes before you've decided anything. That's exactly what just happened to Local Services Ads. If you run Local Services Ads and a bill recently included a charge for a call you never answered, you didn't miss anything. Google changed the rule on purpose, and it's part of a bigger shift in how the whole program works. What happened Google is doing two things to Local Services Ads at once. First, it's retiring the standalone LSA dashboard and moving campaigns into Google Ads itself, as a new kind of Performance Max campaign built around paying per lead instead of per click. The first group of advertisers, mostly US home and storefront businesses like plumbing, HVAC, electrical, and pest control, started migrating in August 2026. A second group, including service-area businesses without a storefront, is scheduled for late 2026, with everyone else following into 2027. Second, and separately, Google changed what counts as a billable call lead. As of October 1, 2026, a missed call during your posted business hours becomes a charged lead if the caller stays on the line for more than 20 seconds, even though you never picked up. Google says the goal is to reward businesses that respond quickly and reliably, since people searching for a plumber or an electrician want to reach someone fast. Why it matters Local Services Ads is pay-per-lead, not pay-per-click, so the definition of "lead" is the entire basis of what you're charged for. Changing that definition changes your bill, and it changes it retroactively from the customer's perspective: the same call that used to cost you nothing because nobody answered can now cost you something because the caller waited. This isn't a vague platform tweak. It has a specific, checkable mechanism, and that's actually good news, because it means you can verify exactly how it applies to your business rather than guessing. How the new billing rule actually works A missed call is only charged if the caller stays connected more than 20 seconds during your business hours, as set in your Google Business Profile. If your ad schedule is different from your posted hours, a missed call only gets charged when it falls inside both. If your phone system routes to an automated menu, the 20-second clock doesn't start until the caller presses a key, and a caller who hangs up without pressing anything isn't charged at all. A call that reaches voicemail or a recorded greeting without a key press, though, is still treated as connected, and can be charged the same way a missed call can. Every lead now shows a clear status in your account: Charged, Not charged, In review, or Credited. Google says it keeps assessing lead quality for 30 days after a lead comes in, and automatically credits ones it decides were poor quality, duplicate, or invalid. If the same customer calls or messages again within 15 days, you're only billed once for that relationship, not once per call. Google's own Ads Liaison, Ginny Marvin, confirmed advertisers "will only be charged 1x" for that kind of follow-up contact. One limit worth knowing: automatic lead credits aren't available for health care or tax-specialist advertisers, or for businesses in the EU/EEA. What else is changing with the migration Separate from billing, the move into Google Ads changes some operational details. Weekly budgets become daily averages. Manual bidding and a per-vertical Target CPA go away, replaced by one campaign-level Target CPA, so a business running multiple service categories loses the ability to bid them differently inside a single campaign. BBB callouts are discontinued, so you'll want at least a handful of other structured callouts ready to take their place. Your business name, address, and hours now sync one-way from your Google Business Profile, and a significant change to any of those can trigger a short verification review, sometimes pausing your campaign for a day or two. What doesn't change: you still pay per valid lead rather than per click, your ads still show up only on Google Search and Maps, and targeting is still keywordless, based on your service categories and areas. Your lead history, including contact details and past messages, carries over, and so does your Google Verified badge. What to actually do If you haven't migrated yet, download or screenshot your historical performance reports now. Once an account migrates, old campaign-level and ad-level performance data doesn't carry over into the new reporting, even though your lead history does. Google sends a notice 14 days before your migration date and a reminder 7 days before, so check that your account administrator's email is current and that someone is actually opted in to lead notifications. If you've already migrated, look at your Leads page and get familiar with the Charged/Not charged/In review/Credited statuses before you need them to make sense of a confusing bill. If a lead looks wrong, Google's feedback survey on that lead is the way to flag it for review. What not to overreact to This isn't Google trying to quietly inflate your bill. The quality-assessment and credit system is still there, the 15-day repeat-contact rule stops you from being charged twice for the same customer, and the IVR exceptions mean a caller who hangs up on your phone tree doesn't cost you anything. If your team is genuinely answering calls or picking up messages promptly, most of this change shouldn't move your spend much. It mainly matters for calls that currently go unanswered longer than 20 seconds, which is worth knowing even apart from the billing change. What to watch next The second migration phase, covering service-area businesses without a storefront, lands in late 2026, with non-US accounts following in 2027. Until Google opens up creating new pay-per-lead campaigns directly inside Google Ads, new LSA campaigns still have to start at g.co/localservices. If your business is scheduled for a later phase, treat the next few months as a preview of what's coming rather than something to act on today, and keep an eye on your migration email so you're not caught by the 14-day notice window. The bigger lesson here Local Services Ads isn't the only place this can happen. Any platform you advertise on, Google Ads, Meta, LinkedIn, even your email platform, can quietly redefine what counts as a lead, a click, a subscriber, or a conversion, and that definition is what your bill and your results are actually measuring. The fix isn't to distrust every platform update. It's to build the habit of reading the actual definition whenever one changes, the way you just did with this one, so a billing or reporting change never catches you off guard again. title: Google Opened Up Real Ad-Impact Testing. Most Small Businesses Still Can't Get In the Door.
deck: Conversion Lift studies used to need a Google rep. Now advertisers can run them directly, but the eligibility bar leaves most small-business budgets outside looking in.
body: Google wants advertisers to know something that sounds a lot like a straightforward win: you can now measure whether your ads are actually working, not just whether someone clicked after seeing one. On October 7, 2026, Google Ads expanded self-serve access to Conversion Lift for Search and Performance Max campaigns, bringing those two campaign types in line with Display, Video, Demand Gen, and App campaigns, which were already self-serve eligible. Conversion Lift is Google's incrementality-testing tool: it splits your audience into a group that sees your ads and a holdout group that doesn't, then compares results to estimate how many conversions your ads actually caused, rather than just assigning credit through an attribution model after the fact. Previously, running one of these studies on Search or PMax specifically meant going through a Google representative. Now, for accounts that already have Conversion Lift access, eligible advertisers can set up a Search or PMax study themselves. That's a real improvement, and it matters for a specific reason: standard conversion tracking tells you what happened after someone saw your ad. It can't tell you whether that conversion would have happened anyway. Incrementality testing is the more honest number, closer to an actual answer to "is this spend doing anything." The eligibility bar most small businesses won't clear Here's the part that didn't make most of the headlines, confirmed directly against Google's own Conversion Lift documentation, not just the announcement coverage. To run a self-serve study on any supported campaign type, including Search and Performance Max, Google requires at least 1,000 observed conversions not counting conversions from supplementary data and a minimum $5,000 budget on the participating campaign. That's the campaign-level bar. There's a separate, account-level one too. Google's documentation states plainly that Conversion Lift isn't available to every account, and that reaching it in the first place still means contacting a Google account representative, the same as alpha and beta campaign types. What changed on October 7 is narrower than "anyone can self-serve now": Search and Performance Max simply joined the list of self-serve-eligible campaign types for accounts that already have Conversion Lift access. Two separate questions decide whether you can actually run a study: whether your account has access at all, and whether your specific campaign clears the conversion and budget thresholds. Compare those campaign-level numbers against where small businesses actually are. LocalIQ's 2026 small-business marketing report found that 52% of SMBs run their entire monthly marketing budget, not just one campaign, under $1,000. Half have no employees dedicated to marketing at all. For a meaningful share of Lonko's audience, a single campaign clearing a $5,000 budget threshold isn't a stretch goal for next quarter. It's a different budget tier entirely.

title: AI Overviews and Local Search: What Actually Changed for Small Businesses
deck: Two business owners can search Google today and land in completely different experiences — and it has nothing to do with luck.
body: Search "plumber near me" and you'll often see a Local Pack with nearby businesses. Search "how do I fix a leaking pipe" and you may instead see an AI-generated answer before the traditional organic links. Search results vary by query, user, location, device, and Google's current systems — but that pattern shows up often enough to matter. It's the distinction that often gets lost in broad headlines about AI and search. What actually happened Google has been rolling AI Overviews — its AI-generated answer boxes — into search results since 2024. By early 2026, research from SparkToro using Similarweb's search panel data for the current figure found that 68% of Google searches now end without anyone clicking a website at all, up from about 60% two years earlier and roughly 45% a decade ago. SparkToro is explicit that this isn't one continuous dataset: the older figures come from different clickstream providers — Jumpshot for 2016 and 2019, Datos for 2024, Similarweb for 2026 — not the same panel measured consistently over time. Treat the long-term trend as directional rather than a precise year-over-year comparison. SparkToro argues that AI Overviews are likely a major driver of the recent increase, while noting that its zero-click measure cannot isolate AI Overviews from other SERP features and changes in user behavior. The clearest evidence comes from Ahrefs. Their original analysis, published in 2025, sampled 300,000 keywords — 150,000 with an AI Overview present and 150,000 comparable informational keywords without one — and found position-one results averaged about 34.5% fewer clicks on the AI-Overview queries. Ahrefs re-ran the same analysis in February 2026, using the same methodology on a fresh 300,000-keyword sample comparing December 2023 to December 2025, and found the gap had grown to 58%. That's a correlation between AI Overview presence and lower average click-through rate, measured specifically within Ahrefs' desktop, informational-keyword sample — an association observed twice using a consistent method, not a controlled test isolating AI Overviews as the sole cause. It's a consistent, strong signal, and it grew rather than shrank between the two studies. If you run a business and depend on Google for customers, that's a genuinely alarming set of numbers. But before you conclude AI Overviews are coming for your business specifically, there's a distinction worth understanding — because it changes the entire picture. Why search intent changes the picture Not every search is the same kind of search, and AI Overviews don't touch every kind equally. Whitespark, a company that specializes in local search, studied three US cities and six local-service industries — plumbers, dentists, personal injury lawyers, optometrists, medical clinics, and real estate agents — to see exactly where AI Overviews were showing up. The pattern was stark: - On local-intent searches — the "near me" kind, often associated with finding a nearby business — a Local Pack the map with business listings still appeared 93% of the time. AI Overviews showed up in only 15% of these searches. - On informational searches — the "how do I" and "what is" kind — AI Overviews appeared in 92% of the informational queries in Whitespark's sample. - On hybrid searches, which mix a real need with a question, AI Overviews appeared 97% of the time. Bar chart comparing how often Google shows a Local Pack versus an AI Overview across local-intent, informational, and hybrid searches — Local Pack dominates local-intent queries at 93%, while AI Overviews dominate informational 92% and hybrid 97% queries. assets/ai-overviews-local-search-what-changed-chart-local-pack-vs-ai-overview.png Source: Whitespark, 540-query local-search study 2025 — 3 US cities, 6 local industries. Not a universal average. Across the full set of local-business-type queries Whitespark tested — combining all three intent types — AI Overviews appeared 68% of the time. That's a real number, but it describes their specific 540-query sample across three cities, not "68% of all local searches everywhere." The intent breakdown is the part worth remembering, because it's the part that actually tells you what to expect. Why this matters for your business The practical question isn't "are AI Overviews bad for search." It's "what kind of searches actually bring me customers?" In Whitespark's sample, local-intent searches — the "near me" kind, aimed at finding a nearby business — continued to show a Local Pack far more often than an AI Overview. For many local businesses, those kinds of searches likely overlap with commercially important customer journeys: "electrician near me," "dentist accepting new patients," "best tacos in your neighborhood ." That's Lonko's interpretation, though — Whitespark's study measured which SERP feature appeared, not which searches actually produced a call, a visit, or a sale. Where you're more exposed is anywhere your marketing or content has leaned on informational searches — blog posts answering "how to" questions, guides, explainers — hoping that traffic eventually turns into customers. That's exactly the kind of search AI Overviews have taken over in Whitespark's sample, and it's the kind of query where Ahrefs separately found the largest click-through declines. What not to overreact to Don't abandon your Google Business Profile, your reviews, or your local SEO because of AI Overviews headlines. Whitespark's data doesn't support that: in their sample, local-intent searches still showed a Local Pack 93% of the time. That's evidence from one 540-query study, not a guarantee for your specific city or industry — but it's a reason not to panic, not a reason to overreact. Don't assume your rankings dropped because something is broken, either. If your position hasn't moved but your clicks have on a query where you'd expect an informational-style result, an AI Overview appearing on that query is worth checking before you assume a penalty or a technical issue — Search Console can show you whether impressions held steady while clicks fell on the same terms. What to actually monitor Look at your Google Search Console data split by query, not just in aggregate. A drop in clicks alongside flat or rising impressions on your informational queries is a pattern that lines up with what Ahrefs and Whitespark describe — a diagnostic clue worth investigating, not proof on its own, since this view of Search Console doesn't tell you whether an AI Overview specifically appeared on that query. Google's newer Generative AI performance report in Search Console is a more direct source once you have access: it shows impressions in AI Overviews and AI Mode by page, device, country, and date — though it doesn't break results down by individual query yet, so query-level investigation still means checking the live search result yourself. It's also worth confirming your site hasn't been excluded from Search's generative AI features in Search Console's settings — an easy thing to overlook. A drop specifically on your "near me" and location-based queries is a different, more direct problem worth investigating separately. It's also worth tracking phone calls, form submissions, and store visits alongside clicks. If informational content stops sending traffic but your local-intent numbers and actual leads hold steady, the AI Overview shift may be costing you less than the headlines suggest. What's still uncertain Whitespark's study covered three cities and six industries — a real, useful sample, but not a guarantee your city or industry behaves identically. Ahrefs' click-loss numbers are desktop-only and focused on informational keywords specifically, not a blanket figure across every kind of search, and they describe a correlation observed across two studies using a consistent methodology, rather than a controlled experiment — a real and consistent signal, but not proof that AI Overviews are the only factor at work. And Google continues to change how and where AI Overviews appear, sometimes month to month. Numbers this current are worth revisiting again before the end of the year, not treated as settled forever. The bottom line AI Overviews really have changed search — just not the way most headlines describe it. Whitespark found AI Overviews appearing far more often on informational and hybrid queries than on local-intent ones in their sample, while Ahrefs separately found AI Overview presence correlated with substantially lower position-one click-through rates in its informational-keyword sample. Put together, the two studies point the same direction from different angles: the searches most exposed to AI Overviews, and to the click-through losses that come with them, tend to be informational rather than local-intent — at least in what's been measured so far. Knowing which kind of search your marketing actually depends on is the difference between panicking over a scary statistic and making one sensible decision about where to spend your attention next. That's the same principle behind everything we build at Lonko: not more dashboards, just a clear answer to "does this actually affect me, and what should I do about it." excerpt: Search "plumber near me" and you'll often see a Local Pack with nearby businesses. Search "how do I fix a leaking pipe" and you may instead see an AI-generated answer before the traditional organic links. Search results vary by query, user, location, device, and Google's current systems — but that pattern shows up often enough to matter. It's the distinction that often gets lost in broad headlines

title: Google Delayed the AI Max Migration — But Not All of It
deck: A closer look at what's actually changing in your Google Ads account this month, what's been pushed to 2027, what it actually does differently, and how to check your own account in five minutes.
body: Google Ads Liaison Ginny Marvin announced in June that Google would delay its automatic migration of Dynamic Search Ads to AI Max — pushing the original September 2026 deadline to February 2027. If you run Google Search ads for a small business and haven't looked at your account since that news broke, you might assume nothing changes until next year. That's only half true. Campaign-level Broad Match and standalone Automatically Created Assets are still auto-upgrading to AI Max this month, on the original schedule — no delay, no separate opt-out beyond what Google already sent. If your account uses either of those, Google isn't waiting for 2027. What Google actually delayed The part that got pushed back is specifically Dynamic Search Ads DSA . Per Google's own Ads Developer Blog notice, DSA campaign creation reopened on June 15, 2026 after being paused for the migration, and the forced automatic conversion of remaining DSA campaigns to AI Max now happens February 1–28, 2027 instead of this past September. Google also plans to send an official reminder notification to affected accounts on January 15, 2027, and reports from PPC Land and Search Engine Roundtable both put the cutoff for creating new DSA ad groups at January 2027 — Google's own post describes that restriction as part of the February migration window without naming an earlier exact date, so if the precise cutoff matters for your account, it's worth confirming directly rather than assuming either date. Google Ads Liaison Ginny Marvin told PPC Land the extra time was meant "to give advertisers plenty of runway and not interfere with the busy Q4 period," since the original September deadline would have forced migrations during October through December — when ad spend and competition both peak for most small businesses. Google also cited ongoing advertiser feedback comparing AI Max's page-matching approach to DSA's more precise targeting, suggesting early test results weren't universally convincing. What's still happening this month The delay only applies to Dynamic Search Ads. Campaign-level Broad Match and standalone Automatically Created Assets began automatically upgrading to AI Max on September 1, 2026, with Google's rollout completing by September 30. That part of the transition was never delayed — it's the same timeline Google set months ago. If your account uses either setting, the upgrade may already be happening to your campaigns whether or not anyone on your team has looked at it this month. What AI Max actually changes in practice Beyond the calendar, it's worth understanding what's genuinely different about how your ads get matched to searches — not just when it happens. Dynamic Search Ads worked by scanning your website's content and matching ads to relevant searches based on your landing pages. AI Max works differently: according to digital marketing agency Footprint Digital's analysis of the shift, it "tries to understand what the user actually wants in that moment" rather than relying primarily on landing-page content as the matching signal. That's a real shift in how much control you have, not just a rebrand. Under DSA and traditional keyword targeting, you were deciding which search term triggers which ad. Under AI Max, keywords function more as guidance for the system than as strict rules, and several previously separate features — search-term matching, text customization, final URL expansion — get folded into one unified system rather than staying independently testable. In exchange, AI Max offers query matching that extends beyond your existing keyword list, ad copy and landing-page selection that adapts automatically, and, per Google, more detailed reporting on which specific headlines and URLs are actually driving results. Worth being honest about the evidence here: Google's own claim is "an average of 7% more conversions or conversion value at a similar CPA/ROAS" when advertisers turn on the full AI Max feature set. That's Google grading its own product. Independent coverage acknowledges "early data suggests improvements" but, as of this writing, doesn't offer independently verified performance comparisons — worth testing against your own account's actual numbers rather than taking either claim at face value. How to check your account in the next five minutes You don't need an agency audit to find out where you stand. In Google Ads: go to Campaigns → Settings , select a campaign, and look for the "Broad match keywords" card. If it's there and turned on, that campaign is in the group auto-upgrading this month. One detail worth knowing: this setting only appears on campaigns already using conversion-based Smart Bidding — if a campaign isn't on Smart Bidding, campaign-level broad match isn't part of its current setup. For Automatically Created Assets, check your account-level automated assets settings the same way. If your campaign type shows as Dynamic Search Ads instead, you're in the delayed group — nothing forces a change until February 2027. Use that runway deliberately: turn on AI Max for one campaign, run it in parallel with your existing DSA setup, and compare results before Google decides for you in the auto-migration window. Either way, the mistake worth avoiding this month is treating "Google delayed it" as "Google delayed all of it." The DSA delay is real. It's just not the whole story. The bottom line Google gave Dynamic Search Ads a real reprieve, but folded that news into the same announcement as a change that was never delayed — and a real shift in how much manual control advertisers have either way. Reading the delay headline and stopping there is exactly how a small business ends up surprised by a setting change it didn't ask for, or misses the chance to test a real change on its own terms. This is the kind of platform shift Lonko watches so a missed setting doesn't quietly change how an ad account spends money — not because it's dramatic, but because it's easy to miss.
